content: The up quark is a fundamental particle described by the Standard Model of particle physics. It belongs to the first generation of quarks and carries an electric charge of +2/3e. Among all quarks, the up quark is the lightest, with a mass estimated to be between 2.2 and 2.4 MeV/c². According to the Standard Model, there are six types of quarks. Ordinary matter, such as atoms, consists of electrons and a nucleus. The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, collectively referred to as nucleons. The up quark, along with the down quark, forms the fundamental building blocks of these nucleons. Specifically, a proton is composed of two up quarks and one down quark, while a neutron consists of one up quark and two down quarks. The theory of Special Relativity explains that the equivalence of mass and energy implies that particles moving at high speeds possess greater energy and, consequently, appear to have greater mass compared to when they are at rest. The strong nuclear force, which binds quarks together within nucleons, is so powerful that the quarks are believed to move at relativistic speeds. As a result, the majority of the mass of nucleons arises not from the intrinsic masses of the quarks themselves but from the energy of the gluon field that holds the quarks together. The existence of the up quark was first hypothesized in 1964 by Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig during the development of the quark model. Experimental evidence for the up quark was later obtained in 1967 through deep inelastic scattering experiments conducted at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC). Hadrons containing up quarks Several hadrons contain up quarks. For example: Charged pions are mesons that consist of an up quark paired with an anti-down quark, or vice versa. The neutral pion is a meson that is a quantum mechanical superposition of an up quark and anti-up quark pair, as well as a down quark and anti-down quark pair. Similarly, the ρ and ω mesons are also linear combinations of these quark-antiquark pairs. Flavorless mesons, such as certain combinations of quark-antiquark pairs, include contributions from up quark and anti-up quark pairs. A significant number of baryons contain one or more up quarks. For instance, baryons composed solely of up and down quarks include the following: The Delta++ baryon consists of three up quarks. The proton contains two up quarks and one down quark. The neutron contains one up quark and two down quarks. The Deltabaryon contains no up quarks, as it is composed of three down quarks.
